examGuide.title: Mental model and derivation
examGuide.body:
Binary search maintains an interval that may still contain the target. Each update must shrink it while retaining a possible answer. Duplicates require lower-bound/upper-bound variants for first or last occurrences. An exact key-probe count differs from counting separate relational tests. Sortedness or monotonicity is a precondition; a rotated or bitonic array needs an adapted invariant.

**Key relationship:** Binary search worst-case comparisons Θ(log n)

examGuide.title: A repeatable solving procedure
examGuide.body:
1. State sortedness and duplicate rules.
2. Write the interval invariant.
3. Check midpoint updates and unsuccessful termination.

examGuide.title: Approach the exam question
examGuide.body: Keep an invariant describing the interval that can still contain the target, and ensure every binary-search update shrinks it. A bitonic array permits peak location plus two monotonic searches in logarithmic time. A property quantified over all index pairs can sometimes be checked using adjacent comparisons.

examGuide.title: Worked problem
examGuide.body:
A sorted array has 31 distinct keys. Standard middle-key binary search needs at most how many probes for a successful search?

**Answer: 5.** A balanced search tree with 31 keys has five levels: 1+2+4+8+16=31. A deepest key is probed on the fifth comparison, giving maximum 5.

examGuide.title: Conditions and edge cases
examGuide.body:
State whether one comparison means one key probe or separate equality/less-than tests; exact comparison counts depend on that convention.

Binary search over an unsorted array has no correctness guarantee.

examGuide.title: Worked question patterns
examGuide.body:
#### Pattern 1 · MCQ

Worst-case successful binary-search probes among 15 sorted distinct keys?

- **A.** 3
- **B.** 4
- **C.** 5
- **D.** 15

**Answer: B.** A balanced search tree with 15 keys has four levels, giving at most four key probes.

#### Pattern 2 · MSQ

Choose true statements.

- **A.** Binary search requires a suitable monotonic ordering
- **B.** Linear search can work on unsorted data
- **C.** Duplicates make every binary search impossible
- **D.** First occurrence needs careful equal-key handling

**Answer: A, B, D.** Duplicates require a modified boundary search, not abandoning binary search entirely.

#### Pattern 3 · NAT

Binary search on 63 distinct sorted keys uses at most how many successful probes?



**Answer: 6.** A perfect six-level search tree has 2⁶−1=63 keys. A deepest successful search uses six probes.

examGuide.title: Work through the supplied PYQs
examGuide.body:
#### GATE 2025 CS2 · Q20 · MCQ

[Open the original question and try it](/#/lesson/searching?tab=practice)

**What is tested:** Linear and binary search. Refer to the original image for complete givens and diagrams.

1. Compare any two distinct elements. The smaller is certainly not the largest element of the full list because the larger compared element already exceeds it.
2. No comparison at all can certify any selected element as nonmaximum in an otherwise unordered list.
3. Thus, for N≥2, **one comparison, A** is both necessary and sufficient.

#### GATE 2025 CS2 · Q41 · MCQ

[Open the original question and try it](/#/lesson/searching?tab=practice)

**What is tested:** Linear and binary search. Refer to the original image for complete givens and diagrams.

1. Find the peak by binary search on neighbouring values; the increasing/decreasing structure takes O(log n) comparisons.
2. Search the increasing prefix and decreasing suffix with binary search. A constant number of logarithmic searches is still O(log n), not O(log²n).
3. The sorted-array special case supplies the comparison-search Ω(log n) lower bound. The optimum is **Θ(log n), D**.
